children: more affordable requires boosting construction productivity rather than relying on central bank interest rate cuts, according to Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City President Jeff Schmid.

Speaking at an affordable housing forum in Kansas City on Thursday, Schmid laid out the scale of the affordability crisis: between 2018 and 2024, the average share of household income needed to purchase a median-priced home jumped from 23% to 33% in metropolitan areas, and from 19% to 26% in rural communities.

In addition to elevated prices and higher mortgage rates, the culprit is the underlying cost of providing housing. "Building a home requires skilled workers, materials, financing, and time. All of these things have become more expensive in recent years," Schmid said, noting that construction methods have barely changed for decades despite technological advances transforming nearly every other industry.

Meanwhile, labor pressures loom large. The average age of construction workers has climbed to 42 from 39 since 2000, with the share over 55 more than doubling to 22%, Schmid noted. Lower expected immigration compounds the problem, as residential construction has historically relied heavily on foreign-born workers. Homebuilders
also face stiff competition for skilled tradespeople from manufacturing, energy, and infrastructure projects—including the massive AI buildout.

"Since the AI buildout began in earnest, we have seen the real wages of electricians grow significantly faster than other workers," Schmid observed, adding that that same AI investment wave is driving up longer-term real interest rates, raising funding costs for builders.

Regulatory delays are amplifying the pain. Permit and impact fees now account for 3.3% of construction costs, up from 1.9% in 1998, while median permitting time has surged by five months since the mid-2000s. With rates climbing, those delays hit harder: an extra five-month wait on a $10M land acquisition loan now costs $415K at current 10% rates, versus $250K when rates sat at 6%.

Schmid identified a few paths forward: expanding factory-built modular housing, modernizing land-use rules to allow "gentle density" such as ADUs and townhouses, and deploying AI to automate building-plan reviews and speed permitting.

But he offered no relief from the Fed itself. "Our price-stability mandate requires that we set the policy rate to control economy-wide inflation rather than favor one sector over others," Schmid said—leaving efficiency gains as housing's only sustainable route to affordability.
